Report Card: Airport Followings

By: Laura Byrne | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
So-called follow-home robberies have been plaguing foreign and local tourists alike on the roads from OR Tambo. We revisit this issue to see what police have managed to do to stop the scourge.

Unique Selling Point:
In June 2017, we exposed an alarming rise in the number of so-called airport followings, in which foreign and local arrivals at OR Tambo are followed home and robbed in their driveways, or along the side of the motorway. We showed that there are numerous syndicates operating from within the airport and spoke to a 'spotter' who helps criminals identify their targets. In July, we interviewed Police Minister Fikile Mbalula, who took responsibility for the issue and promised that the police would come down hard on these syndicates. In the last three months, SAPS has implemented a multi-layered security plan at OR Tambo, which showed promising early results. However, two recent high-profile robberies, followed by a much-lauded arrest of 6 suspects, have raised the profile of this issue again. Carte Blanche takes a look at how effective police intervention has been.

Summary:
July 2017: shortly after we put together our second story, several suspects are arrested in connection with airport followings, as a result of crime intelligence operations and increased security patrols.
Police MInister Fikile Mbalula announces a new tactical security plan, including suspension of several police, airport and tourism officials, vetting of all airport staff and service providers, new police leadership at ORT, and increased security on routes to and from the airport. The plan, it is said, will be a blueprint for increased security in the country's other airports.

August shows more promising results, with several arrests being made in connection with drug and rhino horn smuggling. IN September, ACSA announces a 10.8% profit increase for the year.

Then, on 26 September, 36 elderly Dutch tourists are violently robbed on their way from the airport to their hotel, hours into a 3-week holiday. The bus driver and tour operator are tied up, several of the tourists are punched, and the robbers try to open fire on them. They are severely traumatised and leave the country immediately.

Less than a month later, seven members of an Iraqi delegation are robbed on their way to their hotel. One is wounded and taken to hospital. The suspects make off with jewellery and cash.

The next day, six suspects are arrested following a tip-off. One of them is the manager of a security company contracted to ORT and is wanted for crimes in Limpopo. Stolen items are recovered and a manhunt is launched for a seventh suspect who escaped. Mbalula is quoted as saying the days of airport followings are drawing to an end.

But is this true? Despite a few arrests here and there, two daring, violent and large-scale robberies show that gangs are undeterred. Do these arrests mean the 'cracking' of at least one airport syndicate? What about the investigation of previous cases we showcased?

Basie Vorster Airport follow-home victim

Press Release:


In June 2017, we exposed an alarming rise in the number of so-called airport followings, in which foreign and local arrivals at OR Tambo are followed home and robbed in their driveways, or along the side of the motorway. In July, we interviewed Police Minister Fikile Mbalula, who took responsibility for the issue and promised that the police would come down hard on these syndicates. In the last three months, SAPS has implemented a multi-layered security plan at OR Tambo, which showed promising early results. However, two recent high-profile robberies, followed by a much-lauded arrest of 6 suspects, have raised the profile of this issue again. Carte Blanche takes a look at how effective police intervention has been.

Script:


VO: In June, Carte Blanche investigated the scourge of follow-home attacks on foreign and local arrivals at OR Tambo International Airport.

UPSOUND: Basie Vorster: I was disgusted, I wasn’t half an hour in my own country and I got robbed.

VO: Spotters identify targets walking through the airport. And when the opportunity presents itself, syndicates get away with thousands in cash and goods. Nineteen incidents were reported between January and June 2017. By July, more than 7 new incidents had occurred in just three weeks.

UPSOUND: Devi: Whose responsibility is the slack security – is it ACSA’s or the police?
Fikile Mbalula: It is us – and I take responsibility in terms of the police, it is us.

LINK: Shortly after we spoke to him, Police Minister Fikile Mbalula announced the roll-out of a comprehensive security plan to combat airport-related crime.

UPSOUND: Mbalula: I want to be clear in sending a strong message to criminals and those corrupt officials in cahoots with criminals that your days are numbered.

VO: But has it yielded results? In March, R100 000 worth of luggage was stolen from Basie Vorster’s car when he and his wife stopped for dinner on the way home from the airport.

UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: What’s the latest with your case?
Basie Vorster: Up til now, I’ve had no feedback from the police itself.

VO: Basie says after initial enthusiasm, the police have lost interest in his case.

UPSPOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: What have their responses been?
Basie Vorster: They’ll get the inspector to phone me back. The investigating officer. That’s the guy that will phone me back. And nobody phoned me back.

VO: Jeremy Peters and his family were followed home from the airport in January, and robbed of R300 000 worth of goods. Jeremy also reports no feedback on his case.

UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: What would you then give the police’s grade?
Basie Vorster: If G is your worst, I would give them a G, really. That’s the way I feel.

VO: So from our local victims’ perspective, police communication fails completely with a double F.
But Police spokesperson Brigadier Vishnu Naidoo says some crimes have been solved.

UPSOUND: Brig Naidoo: Those breakthroughs are going to ultimately help us prevent further attacks on visitors from taking place.

LINK: Two recent high-profile incidents involving foreign travellers have raised concerns once again.

VO: In September, 36 Dutch tourists were robbed by men in police uniform on the way to their hotel. Then last week, seven Iraqi delegates were held up. One was wounded and hospitalised, says Iraqi Ambassador Saad Kindeel.

UPSOUND: Ambassador Kindeel: They robbed them at gunpoint, took everything, their luggage, their belonging, their laptops, other valuables.

VO: But six suspects, two linked to the Iraqi robbery, were arrested and appeared in Court this week. Four remain behind bars and police are searching for a seventh.

UPSOUND: Ambassador Kindeel: The matter is still open and we are still liaising with police.
Macfarlane Moleli: What kind of grade would you give them in terms of the work that they have done?
Ambassador Kindeel: Let’s wait until we see the results of the investigation.

VO: Follow-homes haven’t stopped, but prompt police action earns a C. Minister Mbalula also promised airport staff vetting. Several police officers and other employees have been suspended.

UPSOUND: Brig Naidoo: We are finding that members are toeing the line. They are making sure that they are conforming to the regulations. They are conducting themselves in a professional and proper manner, and most importantly doing what is expected of them.

VO: Brigadier Naidoo says there is also an awareness drive educating foreign tourists and the local tourism industry regarding safety.

UPSOUND: Brig Naidoo: The reassurance I can give you is that we will do everything and will continue to everything in our power to make sure that is achieved.

UPSOUND: Macfarlane Moleli: If you had to grade the security plans that have been implemented?
Brig Naidoo: We work on performance agreement from one to five. At this stage I would say 3.5.

VO: Much still remains to be done, but it’s encouraging to see police taking action. Overall, we score you an optimistic D.
